items.title: UK GDPR, Article 9: Processing of special categories of personal data
items.quote: biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person
items.why: The binding rule. Para 1 prohibits processing of the listed categories; para 2 lists ten exceptions and, since 20 August 2025, also requires an Article 6(1) basis (words inserted by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, Sch. 11 para 4). Biometric data is in the list only where the purpose is to identify a person uniquely. Criminal offence data is not in the list; it is governed by Article 10. No outstanding effects shown on the date checked.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 11A: Further provision about processing of special categories of personal data
items.quote: make provision so that an additional description of processing of personal data is subject to the prohibition in Article 9(1)
items.why: The power added by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, s.74(1). The Secretary of State may by regulations add a description of processing to the Article 9(1) prohibition and say which exceptions apply to it (affirmative procedure). It cannot remove an original category. Fully in force 20 August 2025 (S.I. 2025/904, reg. 2(c)). No regulations made under it were found on the date checked.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 1, Part 4: Appropriate policy document and additional safeguards
items.locator: Sch. 1 paras 38-41; read with s.10 and Sch. 1 paras 1 and 5
items.quote: review and (if appropriate) update it from time to time
items.why: What the appropriate policy document must contain (para 39: procedures for meeting the Article 5 principles; retention and erasure policy), how long it is kept (para 40: until six months after the processing stops, and given to the regulator on request) and what the Article 30 record must add (para 41: which condition, how Article 6 is met, whether retention policy is followed). Section 10 routes Article 9(2)(b), (g), (h), (i), (j) and Article 10 through Schedule 1. Text now reads 'the Commission' (S.I. 2026/386, from 30 September 2026).

items.title: Special category data: What are the rules on special category data?
items.locator: Sections 'What does the UK GDPR say?', 'How do the conditions work?', 'What does 'necessary' mean?', 'Do we need to do a DPIA?'
items.quote: If your purpose is not covered by any of the conditions, and you cannot obtain valid explicit consent, you cannot process the special category data.
items.why: Source of the quotation. States that there are 10 exceptions, that five need a basis in law set out in the 2018 Act, that an Article 6 basis is needed as well, and that 'necessary' means more than useful or standard practice. Carries an 'under review' banner following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, and still describes Article 22(4), which has been replaced by Article 22B.

items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure lawfulness in AI?
items.locator: Sections 'What about special category data and data about criminal offences?' and 'Using AI systems to make inferences' (page updated 28 October 2024)
items.quote: you will need to ensure you comply with the requirements of Articles 9 and 10 of the UK GDPR, as well as the DPA 2018
items.why: The regulator's statement that Articles 9 and 10 apply to AI development and deployment. An AI inference is likely to be special category data where the organisation can or intends to infer the trait, or intends to treat someone differently on it, even without reasonable certainty. Carries an 'under review' banner.

items.title: Biometric data guidance: Biometric recognition. How do we process biometric data lawfully?
items.locator: 'At a glance'; sections 'Can we use consent and explicit consent?' and 'How do we determine our lawful basis and special category condition?'
items.quote: If you can’t identify a valid condition, you must not use special category biometric data.
items.why: Explicit consent is likely to be the most appropriate condition for biometric recognition, because no condition exists for identification as such; consent needs a real alternative and is doubtful where power is unequal (employers, public authorities). The 'Key data protection concepts' page adds that biometric data used to infer ethnicity or health can be special category data even where nobody is identified. Publication date taken from the ICO news release of 23 February 2024. Carries an 'under review' banner.

items.title: Enforcement Notice: Serco Leisure Operating Limited
items.quote: Serco has not produced an appropriate policy document as required by Schedule 1, Paragraph 1(1)(b) of the DPA.
items.why: Source of the figure: 2,283 data subjects at 38 facilities (paras 17, 26(i), 39). The regulator found no lawful basis and no Article 9 condition for facial recognition and fingerprint scanning used to record staff attendance: the employment condition does not cover purely contractual obligations, necessity was not shown because less intrusive means existed, and there was no appropriate policy document. An enforcement notice, not a fine; published 23 February 2024. No directory type fits an enforcement notice exactly; 'regulator guidance' is the nearest.

items.title: The Information Commissioner v Clearview AI Incorporated [2025] UKUT 319 (AAC)
items.quote: The decision of the Upper Tribunal is to allow the appeal.
items.why: The facial recognition database case. The regulator's 2022 penalty (£7,552,800) and enforcement notice alleged breaches including Article 9. The First-tier Tribunal held in October 2023 that the regulator had no jurisdiction; the Upper Tribunal set that aside and sent the substantive appeal back for rehearing on the basis that jurisdiction exists. It does not decide whether Article 9 was breached. The First-tier Tribunal had accepted that facial vectors are biometric data to which Article 9(1) applies. The outcome of the rehearing, and any further appeal, was not found.

items.title: The Ryder Review: Independent legal review of the governance of biometric data in England and Wales
items.locator: Chapter 2 (Executive summary and recommendations), Recommendations 1-2; Chapter 5, 'Data protection law'
items.quote: There is an urgent need for a new, technologically neutral, statutory framework.
items.why: Independent review led by Matthew Ryder KC. Its criticism of the present law is the gap a board should know about: special category protection for biometric data applies only where the purpose is unique identification, so classifying people by face or voice can fall outside it. England and Wales only; a recommendation, not law.

items.title: Opinion 28/2024 on certain data protection aspects related to the processing of personal data in the context of AI models
items.quote: The EDPB recalls the prohibition of Article 9(1) GDPR
items.why: International comparator for the training stage. The Board recalls that Article 9 applies to AI models and repeats the EU Court's ruling that a set of data collected in bulk is treated as prohibited if it contains one sensitive item and no exception applies, and that data being public does not mean the person made it public. EU law, not binding in the UK; the Opinion expressly does not analyse Article 9 further. Adoption date as printed on the document.
